title: Books or Bombs? France’s Student Revolt vs. NATO’s Spending Push
content:
By Medea Benjamin

NEW YORK | 12 October 2026 (IDN) — For the third week in a row, high school students across France are taking to the streets demanding more investment in their education. They want more teachers, smaller classes, decent school buildings and a public education system that works for poor and working-class students.

But their struggle comes at a moment when France faces mounting pressure to cut public spending while dramatically increasing its military budget. The question at the heart of this uprising goes far beyond education: Will France invest in its young people—or in missiles, weapons and war? Books or bombs?

What began in the Paris suburbs has spread to more than a thousand schools. On 6 October, more than 250,000 people reportedly took to the streets to support the students.

title: Two African Wars Put Civilians—and the UN’s Authority—at Risk
content:
Ethiopia and Eritrea trade accusations before the Security Council as another deadly strike hits displaced families in Sudan.

By Ramesh Jaura

BERLIN | ADDIS ABABA | KHARTOUM (IDN) — Wars in Ethiopia and Sudan are testing how far the United Nations can act when appeals for restraint are ignored.

Ethiopia and Eritrea have carried their rapidly escalating dispute to the Security Council. Farther west, a drone strike in Sudan’s Blue Nile state has killed dozens of displaced civilians, including women and children.

Although the conflicts have different origins, civilians in both countries are paying for failed agreements and delayed diplomacy.

Ethiopia told the Security Council that Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60 kilometres into its territory. It described the reported incursion as an “all-out invasion” and asserted its right to self-defence.

Eritrea denied the allegation and submitted its own letter to the Council. It accused Ethiopia of manufacturing a pretext for war. It asked for condemnation and “deterrent measures” under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which permits action ranging from sanctions to military force.

title: The Slow-Motion Erasure Of The West Bank
content:
By Dr Alon Ben-Meir*

A people are being erased not in a single cataclysm, but through daily terror: bulldozers, armed settlers, night raids, demolished homes, and stolen water. The West Bank’s suffering is not a security policy—it is a warning of Israel’s own moral collapse

NEW YORK | 10 October 2026 (IDN) — There are crimes that arrive with explosions, and crimes that advance quietly—through a bulldozer at dawn, a rifle at a shepherd’s chest, a child torn from bed, a family denied water until leaving becomes the only way to survive. In the West Bank, dispossession has become a daily ritual and Palestinian anguish a background noise too many have learned not to hear. Homes vanish, villages empty, children tremble through the night, and human beings are reduced to obstacles on land they have called home for generations. This is not security. It is ethnic cleansing, the deliberate destruction of a people’s ability to live.

title: Picasso’s Personal Mythologies: Three Paintings at the Currier Museum
content:
By Sam Ben-Meir*

NEW YORK | 9 October 2026 (IDN) — Manchester’s Currier Museum is currently presenting Personal Mythologies: Picasso in the 1940s and 50s—a small exhibition consisting of three paintings, two of which are on loan through October: L’Homme au béret basque (1946) and The Two Children (1954). The third, belonging to the Currier collection, is the remarkable Woman Seated in a Chair(1941), a portrait of the artist Dora Maar, painted in Picasso’s small Paris studio during the Nazi Occupation.

Maar was a French photographer, painter, and poet, and Picasso’s companion during those years. It is an extraordinarily vibrant painting, bold in its use of line and sharp geometric planes. What makes it truly devastating is hocsso’s brush transforms the simplest of themes—a seated woman—into a psychologically penetrating examination not of Maar or himself, but of their fraught relationship during a period of great uncertainty and immense social and political upheaval.

title: Germany’s Ukraine Policy: The Merz Factor
content:

The following commentary reflects the author’s personal assessment of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s policy towards Ukraine.

title: Breaking the Cycle of Violence
content:
By David L. Phillips*

OXFORD, UK | 8 October 2026 (IDN) — Israel colluded with Hamas for decades, seeing it as a counterweight to Fatah and the Palestinian Authority. Israel’s approach culminated in the terror attack on October 7, 2023 that killed 1,200 Israelis and 252 hostages.

Does Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu bear responsibility for the strategic calculation of colluding with Hamas and the subsequent events? Israeli voters will decide when parliamentary elections are held on October 27.  The outcome will not only determine Israel’s governing coalition. It will also shape society and the future of Israeli democracy for years to come.

Israel made the strategic decision to support the Muslim Brotherhood and Sheikh Ahmed Yassin in the 1970s. However, Yassin’s network of Islamic Schools, mosques and clubs morphed into the Islamic Resistance Movement and the al-Qassam brigades. By encouraging conservative Islamic movements as an alternative to the secular PLO, Israeli authorities had te false hope of weakening Fatah’s nationalist appeal.

title: Brazil’s Fateful Election
content:
By Jonathan Power

LUND, Sweden | 7 October 2026 (IDN) — Since its birth as a nation-state, “Brazil has been a paradise for some, an endless hell for others, and for the rest, a kind of purgatory on earth.” So write two Brazilian historians, Lilla Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, in their massive volume on Brazil.

They continue: “Brazil’s development was born of ambivalence and contrast. On the one hand, it is a country with a high degree of social inequality and low literacy rates. In contrast, its electoral system is one of the most sophisticated and reliable in the world. Brazil has the second-highest number of Facebook users in the world.

“At the same time vast geographical regions lie abandoned, particularly in the north, where the chief means of transport is by rudimentary sailboats. Brazil has an advanced constitution which forbids any discrimination, yet, in reality, silent and perverse forms of prejudice are deeply ingrained and pervade everyday life. In Brazil the traditional and the cosmopolitan, the urban and the rural, the exotic and the civilised walk hand in hand. The archaic and the modern intermingle, the one questioning the other in a kind of ongoing interrogation.”

title: Two Percent of the Christians in Gaza Killed by the IDF
content:
By Benoit Lannoo*

ANTWERP, Belgium | 7 October 2026 (IDN) — On the Instagram account of the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem, Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa reported early Saturday morning that an airstrike on an apartment building in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood of Gaza City had killed, in addition to three other Palestinians, Maysa Abu Dawood and her daughter Mary al-Najjar. The two Christians were very appreciated in the Catholic parish of the Holy Family in Gaza, as they regularly volunteered to help parishioners and refugees who were victims of Israel’s destructive response to the brutal terrorist attack from Hamas, three years ago.

Ceasefire?

Fouad al-Najar, Mary’s fourteen-year-old son, was the first to announce the news of the death of his mother and grandmother. The young man explicitly called for an end to the war in Gaza, because “every day it still kills Palestinians”, despite… a ceasefire from about a year ago. The truce announced by US President Donald Trump on October 10, 2025, indeed can enter the Guinness Book of Records as the bloodiest truce ever recorded. Since then, Israel has effectively murdered another 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza.

title: Germany’s Unfinished Sovereignty: Is Neutrality Still Possible?
content:
By Wolfgang Bittner*

GÖTTINGEN, Germany | 6 October 2026 (IDN) — Recently, there have been calls for Germany to become neutral,[1] as Stalin had already proposed in 1952. At that time, he offered the other three principal victorious powers of the Second World War negotiations on a peace treaty with Germany. The condition was the neutrality of a future united Germany, except for the eastern territories under Polish administration.

At the same time, the Adenauer government had already decided, in secret negotiations, to rearm and join NATO. The Western Allies rejected the Soviet proposal. Konrad Adenauer also dismissed it as an “unserious diversionary tactic” meant to prevent the Federal Republic of Germany from integrating into the West. In this way, Germany lost an opportunity to pursue a self-determined policy.

title: Choosing the UN Chief: The Deals Behind Closed Doors
content:
A study of eight decades of bargaining over senior UN posts raises questions about the independence of António Guterres’s successor.

By Ramesh Jaura

BERLIN | 3 October 2026 (IDN) — The contest to succeed António Guterres as United Nations Secretary-General is gathering pace. Much of the public discussion centres on the candidates, their qualifications and the long-overdue prospect of a woman leading the organisation.

A less visible contest is taking place behind the scenes. Governments—particularly the five permanent members of the Security Council—may be seeking assurances about policies, reforms and senior appointments before deciding whom to support.

A study published by the civil-society campaign 1 for 8 Billion, with the Brazilian research institute Plataforma CIPÓ, examines how such bargaining has influenced the selection of UN leaders since the organisation was founded.

The 41-page report, Backroom Deals: The Trade in Promises for Support between Member States and Candidates for UN Secretary-General, identifies more than a dozen credibly alleged attempts to exchange political support for influence over senior UN appointments.

title: EEPA reports on ENDF capture key towns near Eritrean border
content:
• Ethiopia National Defence Forces (ENDF) and Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) entered Adwa on 11 October. 
  • The Bure, Denakil, Garbo and Awala areas in the Afar region are now considered active combat zones between Ethiopian and Eritrean forces. These clashes involve infantry, heavy weapons and aircrafts. 
  • ENDF and TPF troops are moving closer to the Eritrean border, having captured the towns of Adi Hayelom, Seyemti Adiyabo and Adi Nebrid.
  • Eritrean forces withdrew from Adigrat on 7 October, with ENDF drone strikes targeting withdrawing vehicles. The ENDF and TPF took control of Adigrat between 9 and 10 October.
  • ENDF forces took control of Shire town, northwest Tigray, and of Atsibi and Freweyni, eastern Tigray, on 9 October. 
  • ENDF took control of Idaga Hamus town, Hawzen town and Abiy Adi, northern Tigray, on 9 October. 
  • TPF is allegedly seizing people’s vehicles by force, according to a source in Mekelle. 
  • ENDF fighters are entering and occupying school buildings in Wukro, Tigray, according to a resident on 11 October. 
  • Schools in Egela and Ahza in Tigray were hit and destroyed by drone strikes on 11 October. The responsible party has not yet been identified.
